conversation.content: You are an impartial summarization judge.

Evaluate two candidate summaries against the Human Reference Summary using this rubric: - Content Coverage (0–4): captures main contributions, methodology, key findings - Accuracy (0–3): technically correct, no factual errors - Clarity & Structure (0–2): organized, readable, logical flow - Conciseness (0–1): covers essentials without fluff Human Reference Summary: ${file:documents/arxiv-2508-08314v1/abstract.md} Candidate A: **Paper Title (implicit):** Using Iterative LLM‑Refinement to Generate Course‑Specific Multiple‑Choice Exams and a Large‑Scale Field Evaluation --- ### 1. Main Contributions | # | Contribution | |---|--------------| | **C1** | Introduces an **iterative “Self‑Refine” pipeline** for automated exam authoring. A large language model (OpenAI o3‑mini) alternates between generating a MC‑question, judging it as *good* or *bad*, and feeding the labelled example back into the prompt. This loop continues until 20 acceptable items are collected. | | **C2** | Shows how to **tailor questions to any college course** by feeding instructor‑provided materials (syllabus, description, past homework/exams) into both the generator and the judge. | | **C3** | Conducts one of the **largest real‑world evaluations of AI‑generated items** to date: 71 courses (≈1 200 students) received AI‑written exams; 20 statistics courses (≈ 500 students) received exams assembled from an AP‑Statistics question bank (human‑written) as a benchmark. | | **C4** | Provides a **psychometric (IRT) analysis** of the items, comparing difficulty, discrimination, and overall test information between AI‑generated and human‑written questions. | | **C5** | Openly releases the prompt templates, pseudo‑code, and a full example exam, enabling replication and extension. | --- ### 2. Methodology | Step | Process | |------|---------| | **2.1 Materials collection** | Instructors submit plain‑text versions of course description, syllabus, and any prior assessments. | | **2.2 Prompt design** | Two prompt families: (a) *generator* – asks the model to produce a single MC‑question in JSON; (b) *judge* – asks the model to label the question “Keep” (good) or “Remove” (bad) based on appropriateness, relevance, and non‑triviality. Few‑shot examples from a 2012 AP‑Statistics exam are provided as “good” seeds. | | **2.3 Iterative generation** | Loop until 20 “good” items are obtained:
1. Generate a question.
2. Judge it.
3. Append the (question, label) pair to the prompt as a new example (up to 5 good + 5 bad). | | **2.4 Exam assembly** | The 20 good items are re‑judged for difficulty and answer correctness. The 10 hardest (according to the judge) are kept as the final exam. If <10 survive, another batch of 20 is generated and the process repeats. | | **2.5 Benchmark creation** | For the 20 statistics courses, 10 items are selected from a publicly‑available 2012 AP‑Statistics practice test. Selection is driven by an LLM that matches question concepts to each course and orders by increasing difficulty. | | **2.6 Field study** | 182 sections (164 distinct courses) were recruited across U.S. colleges. 121 sections completed the semester‑end exam; after removing pilot‑created exams, 91 sections remained (71 AI, 20 benchmark). All students also took a common pre‑test of quantitative reasoning. | | **2.7 Psychometric analysis** | A Bayesian hierarchical **2‑parameter logistic IRT model** (item discrimination α, difficulty β, latent ability θ) was fit jointly to pre‑test and semester‑end responses, providing a common ability scale. Posterior inference used cmdstanr (4 chains, 1 000 draws each). Convergence diagnostics (Ȓ < 1.05, ESS > 700) and posterior predictive checks confirmed model fit. | --- ### 3. Key Findings | Metric | AI‑Generated Items | Human/Standard Items | Observation | |--------|--------------------|----------------------|-------------| | **Difficulty (β)** | Mean ≈ ‑0.45 (easier). ~60 % of responses correct. | Mean ≈ +0.35 (harder). ~39 % correct. | AI items were deliberately easier, likely because the generation loop favored concepts that matched the course materials. | | **Discrimination (α)** | Mean ≈ 1.30 (moderate‑high). 31 % “high/very‑high”. | Mean ≈ 1.20 (moderate). 21 % “high/very‑high”. | AI items were slightly more discriminating; posterior difference δα = 0.09 (95 % CI ‑0.09–0.25), with Pr(α_AI > α_STD) ≈ 0.85. | | **Test information** | Max I ≈ 3.85 → reliability R ≈ 0.79; peak at θ ≈ ‑0.51 (best for below‑average ability). | Max I ≈ 2.61 → reliability R ≈ 0.72; peak at θ ≈ +0.32 (best for above‑average ability). | | **Overall reliability** | Across the ability range (θ < 0.75) AI exams provided **greater information** than benchmark exams. | | **Practical outcome** | 10‑question AI exams can be produced in < 5 min of model calls per course and achieve psychometric quality comparable to well‑curated standardized items. | --- ### 4. Limitations & Future Directions * Benchmark limited to courses because suitable public item banks for other domains are scarce. * Only multiple‑choice format was examined; the pipeline could be extended to short‑answer or open‑response items with LLM grading. * Exams were deliberately short (10 items) to limit participant burden; scaling to longer assessments remains to be tested. * The “human” reference condition involved LLM‑mediated selection of AP items, not fully bespoke expert‑crafted exams. * The IRT analysis assumes a static ability (θ) between pre‑test and semester‑end; differential learning gains across conditions could bias comparisons. Future work suggested: (1) randomised assignment of AI vs. expert exams across many subjects; (2) fine‑tuning LLMs on student‑response data to directly target desired difficulty/discrimination; (3) integration with adaptive testing platforms; (4) multilingual and culturally‑adapted question generation. --- ### 5. Take‑away The study demonstrates that **an iterative LLM‑refinement loop can autonomously generate high‑quality, course‑specific multiple‑choice questions** whose **psychometric properties rival or exceed those of human‑written standardized items**, while requiring dramatically less expert time. This positions generative AI as a viable tool for scaling personalized assessment in higher education. Candidate B: **Concise Summary** *Main Contributions* 1. **Iterative, self‑refining AI generation pipeline** – A two‑stage, self‑refining loop that uses instructor‑provided course materials to generate, judge, and refine multiple‑choice questions. The pipeline converges on high‑quality, course‑specific items after producing 20 “good” questions and selecting the hardest 10 for the final exam. 2. **Large‑scale, real‑world psychometric evaluation** – One of the largest field studies of AI‑generated assessments (91 courses, 1,686 students). The study compares AI‑generated items to human‑written items derived from a publicly available AP‑Statistics practice exam. 3. **Demonstrated equivalence (and in some metrics, superiority) of AI‑generated items to expert‑written items** – Using item response theory (IRT) to quantify difficulty and discrimination across a diverse set of courses. *Methodology* - **Data collection** – Instructors supplied course descriptions, syllabi, and past homework/exam content. Students completed a common pre‑test and a semester‑end exam (AI‑generated or AP‑based). - **AI generation** – The OpenAI `o3‑mini` model performed a repeated `generate → judge → refine` loop. The generator prompt included the course text and up to five prior “good” and “bad” examples. The judge (same model) labeled each question as “good” or “bad” based on appropriateness, originality, and non‑logistical content. - **Exam construction** – After 20 good items were produced, a final judging round verified correctness and difficulty. The 10 most difficult, validated items were selected as the final exam. - **Benchmarking** – For statistics courses, 24 AP‑Statistics 2012 practice questions were tagged for concept match and difficulty by the model, then 10 were assembled per class. - **Analysis** – All student responses (pre‑test + final exam) were fit jointly to a hierarchical Bayesian 2‑parameter logistic IRT model (using `cmdstanr`). Priors on discrimination (`α`) and difficulty (`β`) were weakly informative. Posterior predictive checks confirmed calibration. Item parameters were compared across AI and AP question types; test information curves were plotted to assess overall exam quality. *Key Findings* 1. **Difficulty** – AI questions had an average difficulty parameter of \(\barβ_{AI} = –0.45\) (students with below‑average ability had ≈50 % chance of answering correctly). AP questions were harder, \(\barβ_{STD} = 0.35\). The difference is statistically significant (\(E[Δβ] = –0.79\), \(CI [–0.94, –0.65]\)). 2. **Discrimination** – AI questions averaged \(\barα_{AI} = 1.30\) versus \(\barα_{STD} = 1.20\). The posterior mean difference \(Δα = 0.09\) shows a moderate advantage for AI items (\(Pr(Δα>0) ≈ 0.85\)). Nearly 36 % of AI items were “high” or “very high” discriminators compared to 21 % of AP items. 3. **Test Information & Reliability** – AI exams peaked at \(I_{max}=3.85\) (reliability = 0.79) at ability \(θ≈–0.51\), focusing best on below‑average students. AP exams peaked at \(I_{max}=2.61\) (reliability = 0.72) at \(θ≈0.32\). Across the whole ability spectrum (θ < 0.75), AI exams consistently yielded higher test information. At θ = 0 the AI exam provided \(I(0)=3.36\) versus \(I(0)=2.5\) for AP. *Implications* - AI‑generated, iterative‑refined questions can be deployed across many college courses with psychometric quality comparable to or exceeding expert‑written items. - The approach dramatically reduces instructor time while maintaining rigor, \(d\) accessibility, and potential for personalized or adaptive testing. - Limitations (e.g., only MCQs, stat‑only benchmark, assumption of constant ability) are acknowledged, and future work could expand to other disciplines, open‑ended formats, and randomized study designs. In sum, the paper demonstrates a practical, scalable AI pipeline that produces high‑quality, course‑specific assessment items, validated by a large, real‑world IRT analysis showing parity with traditional, expert‑crafted exams.
